newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Balkans in struggle to supply enough bread.
newsitem.headline: Balkans in struggle to supply enough bread.

text.p: Political upheaval, economic turmoil and the aftermath of war in the former Yugoslavia have left south eastern Europe, once rich in grain, struggling to meet bread needs.
Serbia, once the Balkan bread basket, faces a long haul to get harvests back up to historic levels.
Bulgarians have been queuing for bread. The prosecutor general there is investigating whether charges of negligence would be justified against the exfarm minister over exporting too much grain.
Romania, once an exporter, may have to import to cover shortages in the first half of this year.
Croatia is likely to have to import wheat this year, despite an increase in output. Hungary's farmers can't afford fertiliser.

Western experts see imports slowing and harvests getting bigger. But exact figures are hard to pinpoint, they said in response to questions in a survey of the grain crisis in the region by Reuters correspondents.
"Unfortunately agricultural production here is in the hands of God and the entire production relies on weather conditions," said one Balkan government official.

Serbia and Montenegro, present-day Yugoslavia, will take at least seven years to raise output to pre-1991 levels, a senior government official said. The nation faces a shortage after its worst harvest in 25 years and excessive exports last year.
Industry sources say it bought up to 100,000 tonnes from Argentina, France, Germany, Austria and Hungary recently.
Analysts say Yugoslavia needs up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat before the harvest to provide an estimated 2.5 million needed to feed its 10.5 million people plus some 500,000 refugees.

But in 1995, farmers planted scarcely more than half the area sown in the previous year and fuel shortages helped push the 1996 harvest to a record low of 1.5 million tonnes, down from 2.97 million. Yields were the lowest since 1972.

Empty grain stores helped force the government to increase wheat area planted in 1996 to about 850,000 hectares, the 10-year average and Yugoslavia expects to harvest two to 2.5 million tonnes of wheat this year.
Officials estimate that this means there will be around one million tonnes of wheat and as much maize for export by the end of 1997.
In Bulgaria, bread queues and empty shelves have been a daily sight in recent weeks as the country struggled with a grain shortage rooted in uncontrolled exports two years ago.
An interim cabinet which took office on February 13 immediately released grain from reserves.

It also sold forward about 269,000 tonnes of new crop in exchange for immediate imports and machinery, which Agriculture Minister Roumen Hristov says was as much as it could afford without creating future shortages.

Farmers are being pinched between rising costs and low controlled internal prices, although last-minute incentives by the former socialist government meant that autumn sowing was close to a 1.6 million hectare target.
Hristov said the local wheat price at $85-$100 per tonne was well below world levels but controls could not be lifted without measures to protect the poor, which Bulgaria could also not afford.
Input prices have been freed but inflation and a falling currency have hit farmers. For spring sowing, Hristov said fertiliser manufacturers had offered 10 percent discounts.
"We will secure the winter crop and spring sowing to ensure the incoming government does not suffer a grain crisis," Hristov said. Elections are due on April 19.
The International Grains Council has estimated Bulgarian wheat imports for 1996/97 at a high 600,000 tonnes although one trade source said it might be closer to 500,000 tonnes.
The country will use a World Bank credit to buy some 170,000 tonnes and Poland agreed to supply 100,000 tonnes of wheat against exports of the same amount from the new crop.

Bulgaria has granted tenders to Glencore and Bulgaria's Nada to supply 100,000 tonnes against forward contracts to export 134,000 tonnes from the new crop. Another 35,000 tonnes from the new crop have been bartered for combine harvesters.

Hristov, who said Bulgaria now needed only about 70,000 tonnes to cover the gap until the next harvest, has visited Germany but won only a promise of support for efforts to win EU aid. Germany has duly asked EU farm ministers to discuss a Bulgaria's request for 100,000 tonnes of soft wheat as food aid.

In Romania, the farm ministry said a shortage of wheat may force it to import to cover demand for bread in the first half of 1997. The farm ministry has used some 550,000 tonnes from strategic reserves to secure supplies to bakeries.

Once an exporter, Romania suffered crop damage after a long winter so that in 1996 the harvest was less than 60 percent of a 1995 bumper crop of some 7.8 million tonnes, of which 1.3 million were exported.

The ministry has not issued a 1997 forecast for grain crops but data earlier this year showed Romania sowed more than 2.3 milion hectares to wheat and rye last autumn, expecting a wheat crop this year of around 6.0 million tonnes.
Agriculture minister Dinu Gavrilescu said last week Romania planned to set up a hard currency fund of around $60 million for wheat imports to complete the country's reserves if necessary.
Croatia will probably have to import wheat this year, despite a likely increase in production.

After a harrowing experience in 1996, when it exported wheat in expectation of a good harvest only to face disappointment, and stocks turned out to be less than thought, autumn sowings were increased by almost 30 percent.
A big problem in Hungary is that farmers could not afford enough spring fertiliser. Fertiliser usage has fallen sharply since the end of communism.
Farm ministry figures say the fertilised area shrunk to 1.85 million hectares in 1995 from 4.4 million in 1985. In the same period, the fertiliser usage per hectare dropped to 40 kilograms from 220.
Benedek Fulop, state secretary of the agriculture ministry said he hoped that this year per hectare fertiliser usage would grow.
Crop estimates are not available, but the area under wheat is around 1.13 million hectares, up from last year's 1.06 million, with that sown with maize unchanged.
- Compiled from reports by Reuters correspondents in Belgrade, Bucharest, Budapest, London, Paris, Sofia and Zagreb. London Newsroom -44 171 542 7928
